title: Understanding Intent, Buying, Company Signals
summary: Compare intent signals, buying signals, and company signals with examples, a scoring model, and data sources for ABM programs.
body_markdown:
You’ve got a dashboard full of triggers and no clear sense of which ones deserve a rep’s time today. Part of the problem is vocabulary: intent signals, buying signals, and company signals get treated as interchangeable when they’re really three sizes of the same category, each one nested inside the next. Sort out the scope differences first, and deciding which account to work next gets a lot more straightforward.


**TLDR:**


- Intent signals track research behavior; buying signals add funding, hires, and office moves.
- Company signals are the widest tier: every detected event, whether or not it points to a sale.
- Score signals by strength and corroborate at least two types before routing an account to a rep.
- Intent data splits into first-party, second-party, and third-party, each with different coverage gaps.
- PredictLeads Company Signals draws from a company’s own public footprint across 12 categories.


## What Are Intent Signals


Intent signals are discrete data points showing that a specific company, or a person inside it, is actively researching a topic, product category, or solution. A spike in searches for “data warehouse migration,” a cluster of visits to pricing pages across review sites, a surge of content downloads on a narrow topic: each one qualifies. Intent data is the aggregated layer that scores those signals across accounts; the signals are the raw events underneath it, and that specificity is what makes a signal usable for outreach instead of just reassuring for a dashboard.


Self-service preference explains the attention they get. A Gartner survey found that[67%](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-03-09-gartner-sales-survey-finds-67-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-experience) of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience, so signals aim to surface research activity that a rep-free buyer never surfaces through a form fill. A platform engineer comparing API rate limits across three vendors’ documentation pages, without ever requesting a demo, is exactly the kind of activity these signals are built to catch.


## What Are Buying Signals


Buying signals cover any observable event suggesting a company might be ready to purchase. That category includes intent signals, but it extends well beyond online research behavior. A funding round, a new office opening, a leadership hire, a hiring surge in a department that depends on your product: all of these count as buying signals, even though none involve a search query or a page view.


The distinction matters for disambiguation. Intent signals are always digital and always about research activity. Buying signals can be digital or structural, research based or driven by a company event. A company that just raised a Series B and posted 10 new sales roles is[actively hiring as a buying signal](https://predictleads.com/blog/hiring-as-a-buying-signal/) without necessarily having visited a competitor’s pricing page. Treat intent signals as one input into a buying signal, not a synonym for it.


## What Are Company Signals


Company signals are the widest tier of the three. A[company signal](https://predictleads.com/blog/company-signals-hiring-news-funding-technology/) is any structured, detected event about a company’s activity: a hiring surge, a new financing round, a leadership change, a technology swap, a pricing page edit, an office opening. Some overlap with buying signals (a funding round is both). Many carry no purchase intent at all. A company switching its email provider or promoting a VP of engineering tells you something changed, not that anyone is shopping for your category.


That is the key difference in scope. Intent signals track research behavior. Buying signals track purchase readiness. Company signals cover every detectable change in a company’s footprint, whether or not it points toward a sale, and become a buying signal only when the change lines up with something a vendor sells.


## Intent Signals Vs. Buying Signals Vs. Company Signals


The three terms nest inside each other instead of sitting as separate categories. Intent signals are the narrowest: research behavior tied to a topic. Buying signals are the mid-tier: any[sales trigger event](https://predictleads.com/blog/sales-trigger-events-outbound-timing/) , research based or not, tied to purchase readiness. Company signals are the widest: every structured, detected event about a company, whether it points toward a sale or not.

Scope


Example

A single event can sit in more than one tier. An office opening is a company signal on its own, becomes a buying signal for a furniture supplier or staffing firm, and only becomes an intent signal if that company is also researching commercial leases.


Most intent signals qualify as buying signals, and most buying signals qualify as company signals, but the nesting is not universal: the reverse rarely holds, and as the office-opening example shows, a company signal does not always nest upward into an intent signal.


## Types Of Intent Data: First-Party, Second-Party, And Third-Party


Intent data splits into three sourcing categories based on who owns the property where the behavior happens.


- **First-party** : Collected from your own website and product (pricing page visits, repeat logins, feature usage, demo requests). You control collection and accuracy, but you only see people already aware of you.
- **Second-party** : Shared directly from another company’s property, most often a review site like G2 telling a vendor which accounts viewed its listing. Narrower than third-party data, but sourced from one known origin.
- **Third-party** : Sold by vendors like Bombora or folded into ZoomInfo’s intent layer, aggregating research activity across a publisher network you do not own. This is the broadest and hardest to verify category. Coverage depends on whether your target accounts actually browse the tracked publishers, a limitation that[technographic data providers](https://predictleads.com/blog/technographic-data-providers/) face differently since they detect tool usage directly: enterprise accounts active on B2B publishers generate clean signal, while smaller businesses often return nothing. A quiet result does not always mean a quiet account.


## Common Examples Of Intent Signals


Intent signals vary in strength, and grouping them by how close they sit to an actual purchase decision makes the list easier to act on.


**Weak signals (fit, not behavior)**


- Firmographic match: company size, industry, or revenue band aligns with your ICP
- General site traffic from a target account with no specific page pattern
- A contact matching your buyer persona engaging with a generic social post


**Moderate signals (early research behavior)**


- Repeated visits to a blog post or resource page on a specific topic
- Content downloads clustered around one problem area
- Search queries for category terms picked up through[third-party intent data](https://predictleads.com/blog/using-intent-data-b2b-sales/)


**Strong signals (late-stage engagement)**


- Pricing page visits, especially repeat visits from multiple people at the same account
- Comparison or review activity on sites like G2, where a company checks you against competitors
- Demo requests or trial signups


**Contextual signals (not research, but still predictive)**


- Hiring for a role tied to your product category, such as a data engineer posting right before a data warehouse evaluation
- Adopting a complementary technology that typically pairs with yours
- A recent funding round that creates fresh budget for the category


Signals further down this list generally deserve priority in outreach: they sit closer to a real buying window than a loose fit match.


## How To Score And Rank Buying Readiness


A workable scoring model mirrors the tiers above: weight weak signals lightly, moderate signals more, and strong signals heaviest, then set a threshold where an account moves from watch to work. Most teams sum points per signal into a composite score and route anything above a cutoff to a rep.


Accuracy depends on corroboration, not any single number. A pricing page visit plus a[hiring signal](https://predictleads.com/blog/hiring-signals-b2b-sales-account-prioritization/) plus a funding round carries far more weight together than any one alone.


Signal decay matters too. A signal from 60 days ago that nobody acted on is not the same as one from yesterday. Build decay into the score: reduce weight on a schedule, or require a minimum recency window.


Three questions to run against any scoring system:


- Does the score combine at least two independent signal types, or rest on one feed
- Does it discount signals by age, or treat a 90 day old spike the same as a fresh one
- Does it surface the underlying evidence, or just a number with no way to check it


## Intent Software And Tools To Know


**CRM-native buyer intent**


[HubSpot’s Buyer Intent feature](https://www.hubspot.com/products/crm/intent) identifies companies most likely to become customers based on website visits and research activity, then routes them to a rep inside the CRM a team already uses. The advantage is proximity: no second tool to check, no export step.


**Dedicated third-party intent vendors**


ZoomInfo Intent flags a company once its research activity on a relevant topic spikes above its baseline. Bombora’s Company Surge pulls from a publisher cooperative instead, scoring accounts by research volume across a shared network of B2B sites. Both depend on whether your target accounts actually show up in the tracked data.


**Review-site intent**


G2 Buyer Intent captures research happening on G2, including comparison views and category browsing, which tends to run later stage than generic third-party topic data.


**Workflow and outreach tools**


Clay, lemlist, Koala, and Unify do not generate intent data themselves, though several plug into[company signals for lead generation](https://predictleads.com/blog/b2b-lead-gen-company-signals/) by pulling events in from the vendors above and triggering outreach, scoring, or enrichment on top. Check coverage of your target accounts, CRM integration, compliance posture, and whether a match comes with evidence or just a score.


## Common Mistakes Teams Make With Intent And Buying Signals


- **Treating every signal as equally strong.** A firmographic match and a pricing page visit are not the same account temperature. Teams that score them identically end up chasing cold accounts with the same urgency as hot ones.
- **Ignoring recency.** A signal from two months ago that nobody worked is not a reason to call today. Without a decay rule, old spikes look as fresh as yesterday’s.
- **Relying on one data source.** A single intent feed tells you a topic spiked, not who is researching it or why. Pairing that spike with a hiring signal or a funding event turns a maybe into something worth a rep’s time.
- **Over-automating outreach.** Routing every signal straight into a sequence removes the specificity that makes a signal-based email work.


The common thread: treating signals as an answer instead of a starting point for a judgment call.


## Data Sources For Account-Based Marketing Signal Programs


An[account-based marketing technographic data](https://predictleads.com/blog/account-based-marketing-technographic-data/) stack rarely works off one feed. Most programs layer four categories of data, each covering a blind spot the others miss.


- First-party CRM and web analytics: pricing page visits, repeat logins, demo requests. Accurate but limited to accounts already aware of you.
- Third-party intent cooperatives: research activity across a publisher network, useful for catching accounts before they visit your site, though coverage depends on whether your targets browse the tracked sites.
- Technographic data: evidence of which tools a company uses, useful for competitor displacement and integration targeting. A detection shows evidence of use, not confirmation of an active installation.
- Firmographic, funding, and hiring event data: company size and industry fit, fresh funding rounds, and hiring surges in departments tied to your product.


Firmographic data confirms fit but says nothing about timing, which is why teams often route it through[CRM enrichment APIs](https://predictleads.com/blog/best-crm-enrichment-apis-b2b/) alongside other sources. Intent data signals timing but says nothing about budget. Funding and hiring events confirm growth but miss research behavior. Most mature ABM stacks combine at least two of these categories, usually three.

Sorting signals by tier keeps your team from treating a loose firmographic match with the same urgency as a repeat pricing page visit. ## FAQ


### How do intent signals differ from buying signals and company signals?


Intent signals cover only digital research behavior on a topic, like repeat visits to pricing pages or content downloads clustered around one problem area. Buying signals are broader and include any event tied to purchase readiness, research-based or not, such as a funding round or leadership hire. Company signals are the widest tier: every structured, detected event about a company, whether or not it points toward a sale.


### ZoomInfo intent signals vs. Bombora intent signals: which one should I use?


Neither is a strictly better choice. It depends on where your target accounts already sit. If your team already runs on ZoomInfo for firmographic and contact data, the native intent layer adds signal without a new source to manage. Bombora’s cooperative tends to skew toward larger B2B buyers active across its specific publisher network, so it’s a stronger fit when your ICP matches those accounts. Check which network your actual target list shows up on before picking one over the other.


### Is ZoomInfo intent data accurate enough to trigger outreach on its own?


Third-party intent data like ZoomInfo’s is one input, not a verdict: a topic spike tells you research happened somewhere in the tracked network, not who exactly is researching or why. Corroborate it with a hiring signal, a funding event, or a Technology Detection before routing it to a rep, since a single feed showing nothing does not always mean the account is quiet.


### Can I use HubSpot’s buyer intent feature instead of a dedicated intent software tool?


Yes, if your team already lives in HubSpot’s CRM and wants intent data without adding a second tool. HubSpot’s Buyer Intent feature flags companies likely to convert based on website visits and research activity and routes them to a rep inside the CRM, trading some of the broader publisher-network coverage you would get from dedicated intent software for that proximity.


### What’s the best way to find out when a target account’s own activity changes, beyond when they visit a competitor’s pricing page?


Behavioral intent data from third-party cooperatives only tracks a publisher network you do not own, so it misses a target account’s internal changes entirely. Company Signals datasets pull from a company’s own public footprint, including Job Openings, SEC Filings, Website Evolution, and Technology Detections, to flag changes like a hiring surge in one department or a technology swap, each tied to source evidence instead of an aggregated score.
